title: Consider an alternative: mitigating anchoring effects in professional judges’ sentencing decisions
abstract: Abstract We investigate the impact of a cognitive intervention on the anchoring effect in the context of criminal justice, where public prosecutors’ sentencing recommendations influence judicial decisions. We predicted that prompting judges to engage in more deliberative thinking about the prosecutor’s demand would reduce its influence on sentencing decisions. We conducted an experiment on French professional judges ( N = 139) where they evaluated a criminal case in which the prosecutor’s sentencing demands served as anchors. As expected, we found judges exhibited an anchoring effect: they pronounced more severe sentences after high (vs. low) demands from the prosecutor. The cognitive intervention consisted in asking judges to consider an alternative, that is, to generate arguments supporting both the proposed sentence and an opposite (lower or higher) sentence. This intervention substantially reduced the anchoring effect. These findings suggest that judges may rely on the prosecutor’s demands when making sentencing decisions but can be prompted to engage in more deliberative processing. Although these findings should be considered exploratory given the use of a single vignette and the incomplete randomization of experimental conditions across sessions, they suggest that prompting judges to consider alternative sentencing arguments may help reduce the influence of anchoring on judicial decisions. Such simple, effective procedural safeguards may help courts promote fair sentencing.
